subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: Read the shift report. Highlight the findings that need the nurse's follow-up first.

segments.text: New crackles in both lung bases
Reports needing three pillows to breathe at night

rationale.correct: Weight gain, crackles and orthopnea point to worsening heart failure.

perOption.s2: Rapid weight gain suggests fluid retention.
perOption.s10: New orthopnea suggests worsening heart failure.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of deterioration in report.

questions.stem: For each task, indicate every staff member who may perform it within usual scope. Each row may have more than one answer.

rows.text: Measuring vital signs of a stable client
Reinforcing teaching started by the RN

rationale.correct: Scope differs by role; the RN keeps assessment, planning and IV push medications.

perOption.r2:c2: Usually outside LPN scope in most states.
perOption.r4:c2: LPNs contribute data but don't develop the plan.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify scope for each team member.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence about informed consent.

content.template: Before surgery, {{b1}} is responsible for explaining the procedure, risks and alternatives, and {{b2}} witnesses the client's signature.

options.text: the surgeon
the nurse
the client's family
the nurse
the client's child
no one

rationale.correct: The provider explains; the nurse witnesses and checks understanding.

perOption.b1:a: The person doing the procedure obtains informed consent.
perOption.b1:b: Nurses don't obtain informed consent for surgery.
perOption.b2:a: Nurses often witness the signature and confirm the client's understanding.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each nursing action, select the legal term that best describes it.

cells.text: Telling a coworker false, damaging information about a client
Not checking a client's allergy before giving penicillin, causing anaphylaxis
Inserting a catheter after a competent client refused

options.text: Slander
Battery
Negligence
Slander
Negligence
False imprisonment
Battery
Libel
Assault

rationale.correct: Know common torts: slander, libel, assault, battery, negligence, false imprisonment.

perOption.b1:a: Spoken false statements that harm reputation.
perOption.b1:c: Failure to meet the standard of care.
perOption.b2:b: A breach of duty that caused harm.
perOption.b3:c: A threat; here the contact occurred.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who lives alone is going home after a hip fracture repair. For each area, select the actions to include in the discharge plan.

options.text: Remove throw rugs
Install grab bars in the bathroom
Use a low chair without arms
Schedule home physical therapy
Plan the first follow-up visit with the surgeon
Stop the anticoagulant when pain improves

rationale.correct: Discharge plans include home safety and follow-up services.

perOption.c: Raised chairs with arms are safer after hip surgery.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with a chest tube whose drainage changed from serous to 50 mL of bright red blood in the last hour
A client 2 hours after a bronchoscopy who has new stridor
A client with pneumonia whose temperature is 38.3 °C (101 °F)
A client with asthma who needs a scheduled inhaler

rationale.correct: Airway threats come first.

perOption.a: Needs prompt follow-up, but not the most urgent here.
perOption.b: Stridor signals upper airway obstruction from laryngeal edema.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN sees assistive personnel (AP) feeding a client quickly while the client is lying flat. What should the RN do first?

options.text: Wait and report the AP to the manager later
Stop the feeding, raise the head of the bed and coach the AP on safe feeding
Take over all future feedings
Document the observation only

rationale.correct: Supervision includes immediate correction of unsafe care.

perOption.a: The client is at immediate risk.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client from a different culture prefers that the family make health decisions. The client is competent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Insist the client make all decisions alone
Confirm the client's preference and document that the client chooses to involve the family
Ignore the family
Let the family override the client's wishes

rationale.correct: Respect a competent client's chosen decision-making style.

perOption.b: A competent client can choose how decisions are made.
perOption.c: Not respectful of the client's wishes.
perOption.d: The client's own choice comes first.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's employer calls asking whether the client has a drug problem. What should the nurse say?

options.text: "Yes, the client is being treated for substance use."
"I can't share any information about any client."
"Call back after discharge."
"I'll ask the client to call you."

rationale.correct: Substance use treatment records have extra privacy protections.

perOption.b: Information isn't shared without the client's written permission.
perOption.d: May imply the person is a client; better to share nothing.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse receives handoff about a client "doing fine." When the nurse checks the client, the client is pale, sweaty and has a heart rate of 128/min. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document that the handoff was inaccurate
Assess the client further and get help as needed
Call the previous nurse to discuss
Wait to see whether it improves

rationale.correct: Always verify handoff information with your own assessment.
references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Act on a change found after handoff.

questions.stem: A client with COPD is having trouble using an inhaler correctly despite teaching. Which team member can best help?

options.text: Respiratory therapist
Physical therapist
Dietitian
Chaplain

rationale.correct: Use interprofessional expertise for specific needs.

perOption.a: Respiratory therapists are experts in inhaler technique and devices.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: After report, place the clients in the order the nurse should see them.

items.text: A client with a glucose of 62 mg/dL who is alert
A client with chest pain who received nitroglycerin 5 minutes ago and still has pain
A client who needs help to the bathroom
A client with a new tracheostomy who is coughing and has noisy breathing

rationale.correct: Use ABCs, then other urgent needs, then routine tasks.

perOption.c: Treat promptly but airway and circulation first.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which question best starts a root cause analysis of a medication error?

options.text: "Who made the mistake?"
"What happened, and what in the process allowed it?"
"How should the nurse be disciplined?"
"Can we keep this from the client?"

rationale.correct: Root cause analysis focuses on processes and systems.

perOption.a: Blames a person instead of finding causes.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: After a medication error causes harm, the provider and nurse meet with the client. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Hide the error to avoid a lawsuit
Disclose the error honestly, explain what is being done and apologize
Blame another department
Tell the client to talk to a lawyer

rationale.correct: Honest disclosure is an ethical and professional expectation.

perOption.a: Unethical and often against policy and law.
perOption.b: Disclosure supports trust and is expected.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with limited mobility can't get groceries after discharge. Which resource is most appropriate?

options.text: A community meal delivery program
Speech therapy
Cardiac rehabilitation
A new prescription

rationale.correct: Community resources support safe living at home.
references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN is assigning clients for the shift. For each client, choose the most appropriate caregiver.

rows.text: Client with new atrial fibrillation started on a diltiazem infusion
Client with stable chronic kidney disease who needs scheduled oral medications
Client being admitted from the emergency department
Client 3 days after a knee replacement who is walking with a walker

rationale.correct: Assign unstable or new clients to the RN, and stable clients with predictable care to the LPN.

perOption.r1:c1: Titrated IV infusions and unstable rhythm need RN care.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with hypothyroidism who feels cold
A client with Addison's disease who is dizzy, with blood pressure 78/44 mm Hg
A client with type 2 diabetes asking about diet
A client with Cushing syndrome who bruises easily

rationale.correct: Signs of adrenal crisis need immediate action.
references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client asks to stop a treatment that is keeping them alive. The client is competent and understands the consequences. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Refuse to involve the provider
Support the client's right and notify the provider to discuss the request
Tell the family to convince the client
Continue treatment without telling the client

rationale.correct: Competent clients can refuse life-sustaining treatment.

perOption.b: A competent client can refuse treatment.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support a client's right to refuse treatment.

questions.stem: The nurse is unsure about an order written by the provider. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Guess what the provider meant
Contact the provider to clarify before carrying out the order
Ask another nurse what to do and follow their advice
Ignore the order

rationale.correct: Clarify unclear orders with the prescriber.
references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which actions show professional accountability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reporting your own medication error
Keeping your clinical knowledge current
Practicing within your scope
Signing for care another nurse gave
Following up on care you delegated
Leaving the unit without handoff

rationale.correct: Accountability includes honesty, competence, scope and follow-up.

perOption.e: The RN remains accountable for delegated care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate task for the RN to delegate to an LPN in a home health agency?

options.text: Admission visit and plan of care for a new client
Weekly dressing change and data collection for a stable client
Teaching a new diabetic how to give insulin for the first time
Evaluating whether goals have been met

rationale.correct: LPNs provide care to stable clients; RNs admit, plan, teach and evaluate.

perOption.b: Within LPN scope with RN supervision.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with a spinal cord injury at T4 who has a pounding headache and a blood pressure of 200/110 mm Hg
A client with multiple sclerosis who feels tired
A client with Parkinson's disease who has a tremor
A client with a migraine who wants the lights dimmed

rationale.correct: Autonomic dysreflexia needs immediate action.

perOption.a: Autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who doesn't speak English is about to sign a consent form. The provider explained the procedure in English. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Witness the signature
Stop and arrange a qualified interpreter for the provider's explanation
Ask the client's teenage child to translate
Use hand gestures to explain

rationale.correct: Informed consent requires understanding in the client's language.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Ensure informed consent with language barriers.

questions.stem: The nurse disagrees with a provider's plan to discharge a client who seems unsafe at home. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Discharge the client as ordered without comment
Share specific assessment findings with the provider and discuss the concern
Tell the client not to leave
Call the hospital administrator right away

rationale.correct: Advocate through clear communication, then escalate if needed.

perOption.d: Use direct communication first, then the chain of command.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews care for a client in wrist restraints. Highlight the actions that are unsafe.

segments.text: with a time-limited order from the provider
tied the restraints to the side rails
not offered fluids or toileting for 6 hours

rationale.correct: Restraints: bed frame, quick-release knot, regular checks and care.

perOption.s4: Moving the rails can injure the client; tie to the bed frame.
perOption.s8: Basic needs must be met regularly.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each item of PPE, indicate whether it is needed when caring for a client with influenza on droplet precautions (no aerosol-generating procedures).

rationale.correct: Droplet precautions: surgical mask, plus standard precautions.

perOption.r2:c1: Not required for routine droplet care.
perOption.r2:c2: Not needed unless doing aerosol-generating procedures.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is interrupted while preparing a high-alert medication. What should the nurse do after the interruption?

options.text: Continue where the nurse left off
Restart the preparation and recheck everything from the beginning
Ask the client to remind the nurse
Skip the second check to save time

rationale.correct: After an interruption, restart the medication process.

perOption.b: Reduces the risk of errors from interruption.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two clients on the unit have the same last name. Which action reduces the risk of errors?

options.text: Use room numbers to identify them
Add a name alert to both charts and always use two identifiers
Put both clients in the same room
Call them by first name only

rationale.correct: Name alerts and two identifiers prevent wrong-client errors.

perOption.b: Alerts and two identifiers prevent mix-ups.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client taking a new sedative is at risk for falls at night. Which intervention is most effective?

options.text: Scheduled toileting before sleep and a bed alarm
Four side rails up
Dim lights with no night light
Tell the client not to get up

rationale.correct: Combine scheduled toileting, alarms and lighting.

perOption.b: Considered a restraint and can increase injury.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The power goes out on the unit. Which equipment should the nurse check first?

options.text: Ventilators and other life-support devices connected to emergency power
Television
Computer for charting
Bed controls

rationale.correct: Check life-support devices first in a power outage; use red emergency outlets.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which actions protect the nurse when giving oral chemotherapy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear chemotherapy-tested gloves
Avoid crushing or cutting the tablets
Dispose of waste in a hazardous waste container
Touch the tablets with bare hands
Wash hands after removing gloves

rationale.correct: Hazardous drugs need PPE and safe handling even in oral form.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a cough and fever is waiting to be seen and tuberculosis is possible. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client and move them to an airborne isolation room as soon as possible
Leave the client in the waiting room
Wear only gloves
Ask the client to wait outside

rationale.correct: Suspected airborne infection: mask the client and isolate quickly.

perOption.a: Reduces spread of possible airborne disease.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with dementia keeps trying to climb out of bed. Which intervention should the nurse try first?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint
Place the bed in the lowest position with floor mats and check on the client often
Raise all four side rails
Give a sedative right away

rationale.correct: Use least restrictive alternatives first.

perOption.b: Least restrictive measures reduce injury if a fall occurs.
perOption.c: Clients may climb over rails and fall from a greater height.
perOption.d: Chemical restraint is a last resort.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's wristband is missing at the time of a blood transfusion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the client their name and proceed
Stop, have a new wristband applied per policy and complete identity verification before starting
Use the room number to confirm identity
Start the transfusion and fix the wristband later

rationale.correct: Never give blood without full positive identification.

perOption.a: Two identifiers and a wristband check are required for transfusions.
perOption.b: Positive identification prevents fatal ABO errors.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
